docs.title: Choose a route that fits you
docs.text: Your starting point A useful first stop Undergraduate or recent graduate DOE SULI, then direct laboratory postings Master’s student Direct graduate internships; check the opportunities spreadsheet International student without permanent residency Eligibility guide, then international pathways and individual job rules Faculty mentor or department coordinator Faculty guide and Research Internship Advisory Committee Know the name: DOE’s undergraduate laboratory program is SULI — Science Undergraduate Laboratory Internships. “SURI” can refer to unrelated university programs. Check the sponsor before applying.

docs.title: Your next 30 minutes
docs.text:
Pick three opportunities. Write down why each fits your interests, record the official application deadline and timezone, and identify one person who can answer a specific question. Then open the application toolkit and start your checklist.

Program requirements can change. Read the sources for uptodate info.

docs.title: Research Internship Advisory Committee
docs.text: The Research Internship Advisory Committee is a faculty contact group for brief advice on national laboratory research internships, as members’ schedules allow.

docs.title: Members & contact information
docs.text:
Start with the student guide and opportunity spreadsheet. If you still have a question, email a relevant committee member with your major, research interest and one specific question.

Member Department / academic unit Email Official UCO source Gang Xu School of Engineering — Biomedical Engineering; Associate Dean, College of Mathematics and Science GXu@uco.edu UCO profile Jyotisna Saxena Department of Biology jsaxena@uco.edu UCO profile Tej Lamichhane School of Engineering — Engineering Physics tlamichhane@uco.edu UCO faculty directory Sean Laverty Department of Mathematics and Statistics SLaverty@uco.edu UCO profile Eric Eitrheim Department of Chemistry eeitrheim@uco.edu UCO profile Christopher Schafer Department of Biology cschafer1@uco.edu UCO faculty directory John Rhee Department of Computer Science jrhee2@uco.edu UCO profile — Junghwan “John” Rhee

docs.title: What the committee can help with
docs.text:
• Offer brief advice on research interests and suitable internship pathways.
  • Point students toward relevant faculty or official program contacts when possible.
  • Share useful opportunities as they become available.

Support depends on each member’s availability. Students manage their own applications, deadlines and follow-up. Contact the internship program office for official eligibility, application-system or selection questions.

docs.title: Find the right eligibility route
docs.text: Check eligibility at two levels: the program’s funding and academic rules, then the specific position and laboratory-access rules. A lab may host one program limited to citizens/permanent residents and another open to some other noncitizens.

docs.title: Understand common eligibility categories
docs.text:
Category What it means What to do U.S. citizen / permanent resident The cited route lists these groups Verify all academic rules and host access; permanent residency is not citizenship. U.S. citizen The cited route lists citizenship as a requirement Do not assume a work permit or permanent residency is a substitute. International pathway The source describes some noncitizen participation or U.S. work-authorized applicants Confirm the job’s exact citizenship, access and authorization conditions; this does not promise sponsorship. Confirm with program The overview does not resolve citizenship for the route Ask the program office before assuming eligibility.

These categories are research aids, not individual eligibility decisions. Citizens may qualify for international pathways too. Permanent residents should consider both citizen/LPR routes and other routes that meet their circumstances. Use the shared opportunities spreadsheet to find programs to investigate.

docs.title: Five questions before you apply
docs.text:
1. Academic level: Does the program accept your degree level and year? Are recent graduates or terminal master’s students included?
  2. Enrollment and performance: What enrollment, credits, GPA, age and graduation-date rules apply, and when must you satisfy them?
  3. Citizenship category: What status does the specific announcement require at application, selection or start?
  4. Authorization and access: What work/participation authorization and site approvals are needed? Who confirms these?
  5. Participation constraints: Can you attend all dates? Are there previous-participation limits, advisor approvals or institutional restrictions?

docs.title: Routes to investigate
docs.text:
U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents: investigate SULI, CCI, SCGSR and eligible direct positions. SULI is an undergraduate/recent-graduate route; SCGSR requires PhD candidacy and thesis alignment. Their requirements are different.

Other noncitizens: begin with specific positions in routes that describe international or work-authorized applicants, including LANL student programs, Sandia’s internship FAQ, LLNL student hiring, INL internships, SLAC summer internships and NETL’s program table. Restrictions differ even within one lab.

Community college students: compare CCI with any direct technical roles that explicitly accept your enrollment. Do not use a four-year-only posting as evidence of community-college eligibility.

Faculty teams: read the current VFP eligibility rules. Institutional criteria and faculty/student criteria are separate. Do not assume every university can participate.

docs.title: Ask a precise question
docs.text:
I am considering [program/job ID] for [term]. I am a [degree/year]
student at [institution]. The announcement says [quote or describe
the unclear criterion]. Does this opportunity accept applicants in
[relevant category], and which office should confirm any additional
authorization or site-access requirements before the start date?

Use an appropriate level of detail in the first inquiry; share sensitive records only through the designated secure process. University international staff and the lab’s authorized office should resolve individual authorization questions.

docs.title: Frequent mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating all DOE programs as having the same citizenship rules.
  • Assuming permanent residents and students on visas are the same eligibility category.
  • Reading “no clearance required” as a guarantee of unrestricted access.
  • Assuming a mentor can waive a funding, employment or site-access rule.
  • Applying with a future status that the program requires you to hold now.
  • Using an old program page as proof of a current opening.

When requirements are unclear or appear inconsistent, cite the exact announcement and ask the official program office. Record its answer and date in your private tracker.

docs.title: Faculty guide
docs.text: Faculty can turn an unfamiliar application process into a reachable research opportunity. The highest-value support is usually a specific assessment of research fit, an evidence-rich recommendation and a timely introduction when a real connection exists.

docs.title: Advise students early
docs.text:
At the start of the recruitment cycle, ask students about their interests, academic preparation, dates and constraints. Help them distinguish undergraduate internships, graduate direct appointments, doctoral thesis awards and faculty-led collaborations. Refer personal authorization questions to the appropriate university and laboratory offices.

Offer a short meeting with three outputs: a realistic program shortlist, one skill to strengthen and a document/recommendation timeline. Students without prior research can start with course projects, independent study or a campus research assistant role.

docs.title: Write a specific recommendation
docs.text:
Confirm that you can meet the deadline and write a strong, honest letter. Review the prompt and student’s recommender packet. Submit through the official system yourself.

A useful structure is:

  1. Relationship and context: how long and in what setting you observed the student.
  2. Technical evidence: a concrete project, method, analysis or result, with the student’s individual role.
  3. Research behavior: curiosity, response to uncertainty, troubleshooting, reliability and follow-through.
  4. Teamwork and communication: a directly observed example.
  5. Readiness and fit: why this opportunity is a reasonable next step, with any comparison grounded in an honest reference group.
  6. Closing assessment: your support and willingness to answer follow-up questions.

Avoid unsupported rankings, generic superlatives, demographic assumptions or copied claims you cannot verify. Discuss a weakness only with context and relevance. Respect confidentiality and application instructions.

docs.title: Illustrative letter scaffold
docs.text:
Dear Selection Committee,

I recommend [student] for [program]. I supervised/taught [student]
in [context] during [period], which allowed me to observe [skills].

In [project], [student] was responsible for [specific contribution].
When [technical difficulty] occurred, they [observed action], leading
to [verified result or learning]. This showed [research quality].

In working with [team/context], they [specific communication or
collaboration example]. Their preparation in [skills] and interest in
[research area] make [program] an appropriate next step.

[Grounded overall assessment and any relevant context.]
Sincerely,
[Faculty name, title, institution, professional contact]

The scaffold is a starting point for the recommender, not a ready-made assessment. Replace every placeholder with truthful, observed evidence.

docs.title: Introduce students thoughtfully
docs.text: Ask the student before sharing their materials. Send a short introduction only when you have a relevant connection: the student’s preparation, the research match and a bounded request. Let the lab researcher decide capacity and fit. An introduction does not substitute for the formal application.

docs.title: Develop a laboratory collaboration
docs.text:
Start with a one-page concept: shared scientific question, complementary expertise, proposed methods, feasibility, required facilities and a potential student contribution. Contact a relevant lab scientist using an official channel, then discuss scope, mentoring time, funding, access and deliverables.

For SCGSR, coordinate with the student and lab collaborator on a defined thesis-related proposal and advisor support. Check restrictions on prior collaboration and the current solicitation before settling on the team.

For VFP, first verify faculty citizenship/employment and institutional eligibility. Current rules generally exclude R1/R2 institutions under the cited classification, with an HBCU exception. Confirm the current details directly. Develop the proposal with the lab scientist and follow separate student rules if including students.

docs.title: Optional application support
docs.text: Session Focus Student leaves with 1 · Opportunity fit Degree level, research areas, eligibility and dates Three plausible routes and unresolved questions 2 · Research story Resume and one project explanation A revised evidence-based application paragraph 3 · Recommendations Writer selection and submission process Complete reference packet and confirmed writers 4 · Interview practice Technical explanation and mentor questions Feedback and a targeted practice plan

docs.title: Sustain the pipeline
docs.text: When time permits, share relevant opportunities or suggest a useful faculty or program contact. The Research Internship Advisory Committee can offer brief guidance as members’ schedules allow. Students remain responsible for their applications and deadlines.

docs.title: Sources & editorial upkeep
docs.text: This independent guide is for planning. Official program pages, current job postings and program offices determine requirements and selections. It is not affiliated with DOE or any laboratory. Suggested preparation and outreach timing are editorial advice, not universal program requirements.

docs.title: Shared opportunity list
docs.text:
Browse the shared opportunities spreadsheet. Listings are maintained there, separately from this website. Spreadsheet edits do not require rebuilding MkDocs.

Verify each listing against its official announcement. Record the program, laboratory, academic level, citizenship/eligibility, application timing, official URL, last-reviewed date and active/paused/archived status. Spreadsheet access follows its Google sharing settings.

docs.title: Official application references
docs.text:
The guide’s initial research was reviewed November 9, 2026. Check current instructions before applying.

  • SULI eligibility, application instructions and FAQs.
  • CCI eligibility and application instructions.
  • SCGSR eligibility and FAQs.
  • Visiting Faculty Program eligibility.
  • Sandia internship requirements and FAQs.
  • Oak Ridge Research Student Internships.
  • Los Alamos student programs.
  • LLNL student hiring overview.
  • Idaho National Laboratory internships.
  • SLAC summer internships.
  • NETL internship programs.

docs.title: Maintain the guide
docs.text:
1. Keep the Research Internship Advisory Committee’s listed contact details current.
  2. Update opportunity listings in the shared spreadsheet. Review promoted deadlines and eligibility against the official program page before sending reminders.
  3. Edit website guidance in docs/, then run mkdocs build --strict. There is no opportunity-directory generator to run.
  4. If a requirement is unclear, ask the program office and mark it as needing confirmation. Do not infer citizenship eligibility from a laboratory name.
  5. Review guidance and contact information each semester. Collect optional, anonymized feedback about confusing application steps.

The application checklist is stored locally in the visitor’s browser. This website does not submit applications or change spreadsheet permissions.

docs.title: Templates & application tracker
docs.text: Use these working documents to organize the process. Customize them for each program and keep your own copy. Nothing here sends an email or submits an application.

docs.title: Download your working files
docs.text:
• Application tracker · Excel — deadlines, job IDs, mentor outreach, letters, interviews and next actions.
  • Shared opportunities spreadsheet — browse the separately maintained opportunity list.
  • Email and research-brief templates · TXT — editable outreach, recommendation request, follow-up and interview notes.

Download the Excel (.xlsx) files and open them in Microsoft Excel, or import them into Google Sheets. Save your own copy before adding information. Keep sensitive identity and immigration records in the appropriate secure institutional process.

docs.title: Request a recommendation
docs.text:
Subject: Recommendation request — [program], due [date, time, timezone]

Dear Professor [Name],
I am applying to [program/host] to explore [research topic]. Would you
be willing to write a strong recommendation based on my work in
[course/project/research context]?

The official deadline is [date/time/timezone], and the letter must be
submitted through [portal instructions]. I can send my resume,
academic record, draft statement and a short reminder of our work
together. I would be glad to meet if useful.

I understand if your schedule does not allow this. Thank you for
considering my request.
Best,
[Name]

docs.title: One-page research-fit brief
docs.text:
Name / degree / institution / available dates:
Program and official URL / job ID:
Research group and potential mentor:
Research question I want to explore:
Recent paper/project and one method or finding I understood:
Relevant preparation and my individual contribution:
Evidence (result, code, report or course project):
What I can contribute now:
What I need to learn:
One feasible project direction or question:
Eligibility or practical questions for the program office:
Next action and date:

docs.title: Application quality check
docs.text:
Read your application as a reviewer. Can they identify the scientific question, your contribution, evidence of preparation and reason for choosing the host? Is the writing direct and accurate? Do the filenames, dates and program names match?

Check the official portal for required letters, submitted status and confirmation. Keep an exported or saved copy where allowed.

docs.title: Interview notes
docs.text:
Program / lab / job ID:
Interviewer names and roles:
Date / time / timezone / format:
Two-minute introduction:
Technical project to explain:
Examples: troubleshooting / teamwork / learning:
Questions: scope / supervision / deliverables / dates:
Program-office questions: funding / housing / access:
Materials promised:
Expected next step and timeline:
Thank-you sent:
Follow-up action and date:

See mentor outreach for first-contact emails and interviews for thank-you and status follow-up guidance. Faculty can use the recommendation scaffold as a structure for their own assessment.

docs.title: Documents & recommendations
docs.text: Build a reusable evidence folder, then tailor the contents for each application. The official announcement determines which documents are required. Do not upload an extra document simply because it appears in this planning list.

docs.title: Prepare your application folder
docs.text:
Item What to prepare Quality check Resume or CV Education, relevant skills, projects, work, research, service and selected achievements One or two pages is often enough for an undergraduate; a graduate research CV may be longer. Follow program rules. Academic records Current and prior transcripts required by the program Legible PDF, your name, institution, relevant terms and grades; check official/unofficial requirement. Research/personal responses A tailored answer to every prompt Specific evidence, correct lab names and exact word/character limits. Research-interest brief One page linking your interests to potential groups Problem, relevant preparation, host fit and questions; submit only if requested. Portfolio A small selection of code, reports, posters or designs Working links and clear individual contributions; share only material you may disclose. Recommendation plan Required number, agreed writers and due dates Confirm portal invitations and received status. Availability/enrollment Academic calendar, anticipated graduation and enrollment evidence if required Consistent dates across application and resume. Identity/authorization records Only what the official onboarding or application process requests Use the designated secure channel; keep these out of outreach packets.

Use filenames such as Lastname_Firstname_Resume_2027.pdf. Keep a private copy of each submitted application and a dated master resume.

docs.title: Write a convincing research statement
docs.text:
Start with a real research question. Describe a relevant experience, your specific contribution, a result or limitation, and how it prepares you for the host’s work. Connect to a group’s method or project without pretending to know its unpublished plans.

Weak: “Your world-class laboratory is my dream.”

Stronger: “In a class project I compared two solvers for a heat-transfer model and found the mesh choice changed runtime substantially. Your group’s work on numerical methods for energy systems makes me interested in learning how you validate those tradeoffs on larger simulations.”

This is an illustrative example, not a claim about a particular lab. Replace it with your own evidence.

docs.title: Choose recommendation writers
docs.text:
Choose faculty, research supervisors or other eligible writers who know your work and can describe concrete examples. Follow the program’s restrictions on who may serve. A detailed letter from someone who supervised a project can be more informative than a generic letter from someone with a prominent title.

Ask 4–6 weeks ahead where possible. If the answer is hesitant, give the writer room to decline and find another eligible recommender. The number of letters differs: SULI instructions specify two online recommendations; other programs use different requirements.

docs.title: Build a recommender packet
docs.text:
Send one organized message or folder containing:

  1. Program name, official URL, selection criteria and exact deadline/timezone.
  2. Resume/CV, relevant transcript and draft responses if helpful.
  3. A short account of how the writer knows you: course/project, term and specific work.
  4. Three factual examples of initiative, technical growth, teamwork or reliability.
  5. Your research interests, host fit and intended next academic step.
  6. Portal instructions, submission method and your contact information.

Provide evidence and context. The recommender writes and submits their own honest assessment. Follow confidentiality and waiver instructions in the application.

docs.title: Track letter submission
docs.text:
Check that the portal invitation reached the correct address. A polite reminder roughly one to two weeks before the deadline is reasonable if a letter remains outstanding. State the deadline and include the submission instructions again. Escalate portal failures to the program office before the deadline.

For WDTS programs, use the required online recommendation process. Do not assume an emailed attachment will count. See the CCI instructions for its submission rules.

Thank writers after submission and share the outcome later. If selected, tell them what you learned; that closes the mentoring loop.

docs.title: Interviews & follow-up
docs.text: The format varies by group: a short mentor call, technical discussion, project presentation or several interviews. Ask the coordinator about length, participants, format and any materials to prepare.

docs.title: Prepare three research stories
docs.text:
Have a two-minute introduction and three examples ready: a technical contribution, a setback and recovery, and a collaboration. Use context → your role → action → result → lesson. Make your individual contribution clear even when discussing team work.

For a five-minute project explanation, cover the question, why it mattered, your method, the result, limitations and what you would try next. Explain figures and units. Prepare to discuss an unexpected result or a failed approach.

docs.title: Practice likely questions
docs.text:
Question A useful answer includes Why this group? A specific research connection and a realistic learning goal Walk me through a project. The problem, your work, evidence and limitations How did you debug or troubleshoot it? A systematic process and what you checked first What do you do when you do not know an answer? Clarifying assumptions, research, asking for help and checking the result How do you work with others? A concrete example of communication and responsibility What can you contribute this summer? Skills supported by evidence and a willingness to learn When are you available? Dates, course obligations and known constraints

Technical preparation should follow the actual position: coding and data analysis, experimental methods, instrumentation, modeling, writing or other relevant skills. Think aloud when appropriate, clarify assumptions and say when you do not know. Do not disclose restricted work from another project.

docs.title: Ask questions that help you evaluate the match
docs.text:
• What would a successful first month and final deliverable look like?
  • Who provides day-to-day mentoring, and how often does the team meet?
  • What skills should I strengthen before arriving?
  • What training, equipment or computing access will I need?
  • Is the project suitable for a poster, thesis chapter or publication, and what review is required?
  • Which dates, location and onsite expectations apply?
  • Who can answer funding, housing, travel, authorization and onboarding questions?

Ask the program office about appointment conditions when the mentor is not responsible for them. Graduate students should involve their home advisor in scope and publication discussions.

docs.title: After the interview
docs.text:
Send a short, individualized thank-you within a day or two. Mention one discussion point, restate interest and provide any promised material. Record the contact and decision timeline.

Subject: Thank you — [position/program]

Dear [Name],
Thank you for discussing [project] with me today. I especially enjoyed
learning about [specific point]. The connection to my experience in
[relevant work] strengthened my interest in the opportunity.

As promised, here is [requested link/material]. Please let me know if
you need anything else. I look forward to hearing about next steps.
Best,
[Name]

If the stated response date passes, send a brief status inquiry. If no timeline was given, a polite check-in after about two weeks can be reasonable. Follow published program instructions if they differ.

docs.title: If you are selected, waitlisted or declined
docs.text:
Selected: request the written appointment details and follow the offer checklist. Give recommenders a brief update and promptly withdraw other applications once you have committed, following program rules.

Waitlisted: confirm whether an action is needed, keep records current and continue pursuing other eligible routes.

Declined: thank the program and ask whether feedback is available. A lack of feedback is common. Review research fit, preparation and timing with a faculty mentor, then plan the next cycle.

docs.title: Offers & onboarding
docs.text: A mentor’s positive conversation is encouraging; the formal appointment documents establish the actual terms. Read them and ask the program office about unclear conditions before committing.

docs.title: Review the written offer
docs.text:
Confirm Questions to resolve Research and supervision Project, mentor, daily supervisor, expected deliverable and review process Dates and work arrangement Start/end, weekly hours, site, onsite/remote expectations and academic conflicts Funding Wage or stipend, payment schedule, housing/travel support, reimbursement timing and personal upfront costs Appointment conditions Access approval, employment or participation documentation, screening and required training Academic coordination Thesis or course credit, university approval, registration, home funding and advisor agreement Practical needs Housing, transport, accessibility arrangements, insurance or health requirements when applicable

Program benefits differ. Do not assume housing, relocation or international travel is covered. Ask for terms in writing and budget for any gap before the first payment.

docs.title: Complete official onboarding
docs.text:
Respond promptly to the designated hiring, program and site-access staff. Only submit identity, immigration, banking or similar records through the authorized process. Confirm requirements with the program office when a request is unclear.

International students should coordinate their individual work-authorization process with the university international office and the lab’s designated staff. An offer or a mentor’s invitation does not itself authorize work or access. Start only when the required approvals and official start instructions are in place.

Arrange housing and transportation around the confirmed dates and site. Some laboratories are difficult to reach without a car; ask the current program about options. Understand cancellation terms before paying deposits.

docs.title: Before your first day
docs.text:
Ask your mentor for two or three background readings, the expected software or methods, and what you should avoid setting up independently. Confirm arrival location, badge instructions, contact person and the first-week schedule.

For graduate research, agree on how lab work connects to the thesis, how often both advisors will meet, and how data, code, authorship and publication review will be handled.

docs.title: During and after the appointment
docs.text:
In the first week, agree on a manageable project scope and regular mentor meetings. Keep a research notebook and weekly progress summary. Ask early about unclear methods or access. Follow site safety, security, data and publication procedures.

Before leaving, complete required reports or presentations, hand off code and documentation, confirm what you can share publicly and return equipment. Thank mentors and recommenders, update your resume accurately and volunteer to share approved lessons with your department’s next cohort.

docs.title: Find & contact a research mentor
docs.text: An effective message shows that you understand enough of the research to ask a useful question. It should make it easy for the recipient to see your preparation, availability and intended application route.

docs.title: Contact the right person
docs.text:
Your question Contact first Include Am I eligible? Which portal or deadline applies? Program coordinator or student education office Program, academic level and the specific unclear requirement Does this job accept my work-authorization category? Recruiter/program office, alongside your university international office Job ID and precise question; use a secure channel for records Does my interest fit a research group? Researcher or group lead using their official public contact One relevant paper/project, your contribution and an attainable question Can I align this with my degree or thesis? Faculty advisor or graduate program director Proposed dates, research scope and degree obligations Who might suggest a research contact? Faculty mentor or Research Internship Advisory Committee member, as available Your research interest and one specific question; introductions depend on existing connections and availability

Use official staff directories, publication correspondence addresses or program contacts. Do not guess private email addresses. Ask the program office to route your question if no appropriate research contact is public.

docs.title: Prepare before you write
docs.text:
Read the group’s official research page and one or two recent papers or project summaries. Note the research problem, method, one result, and one limitation or question. You do not need to understand every equation; distinguish what you know from what you hope to learn.

Make a simple fit table: group / current question / your evidence / possible contribution / contact / route. Choose a few strong matches and personalize each message.

docs.title: First-contact email
docs.text:
Subject: [Program or job ID] — interest in [specific research topic]

Dear Dr. [Name],

I am a [year/degree] student in [field] at [institution], preparing
to apply for [program/position] for [term; dates].

I read your [paper/project title] and was interested in [specific
method or finding]. In [course/research/project], I [your concrete
action and result]. That experience makes me interested in [question
or small contribution connected to the group's work].

Are you expecting to mentor students through [route], or is there a
program contact you recommend? If useful, I would welcome a brief
conversation about research fit. My resume is attached [if appropriate].

Thank you for your time,
[Name, degree, institution, professional contact, portfolio if useful]

Keep the initial message concise, often around 150–200 words. Attach a small resume PDF if appropriate; do not send identity documents, full application bundles or confidential research. Use accurate terms such as “introductory Python experience.”

docs.title: Timing and follow-up
docs.text:
For programs needing a co-developed proposal, begin several months before the deadline. For direct internships, reach out once you have a clear fit and a relevant opening or program route. Required collaborator arrangements should follow the current program’s instructions.

If there is no response, one brief follow-up after roughly 7–10 business days is a reasonable courtesy. This is suggested etiquette, not a lab rule. After that, try a different appropriate contact or proceed with the formal application if allowed. A researcher’s silence is not an application decision.

Dear Dr. [Name],
I am following up on my message below about [specific topic/program].
I remain interested in [one sentence of research fit]. If you are not
the right contact, I would appreciate a pointer to the program office.
Thank you for considering my question.

Outreach does not guarantee selection. Never claim a researcher has agreed to supervise you unless they explicitly have.

docs.title: Program-specific contact routes
docs.text:
• Sandia: use the internship overview and careers links and include the job ID.
  • Oak Ridge: use the RSI page for program questions; approach a research group with a specific project connection.
  • SULI/CCI: use WDTS for application-system questions and the host education office for host-specific research or site-access questions.
  • SCGSR: coordinate a defined thesis project with your graduate advisor and a lab scientist before submitting; see the eligibility requirements.
  • Faculty collaborations: use the faculty guide to prepare a project concept before contacting a prospective collaborator.

docs.title: Your application roadmap
docs.text:
You do not need a published paper to begin. You need evidence that you can learn, contribute and explain your interest in a particular research problem. Course projects, laboratory classes, campus jobs and independent work can all provide that evidence.

The timing below is a planning recommendation. Program deadlines, required letters and appointment lengths come from the current official announcement.

docs.title: 1. Set your constraints · 4–6 months ahead
docs.text:
Write down your academic level, expected graduation date, available dates, research interests, geographic constraints and funding needs. Privately check citizenship and work-authorization categories against the program rules. Use the eligibility guide before spending time on an ineligible application.

For graduate students, meet your advisor early to discuss thesis alignment, time away, funding overlap, university registration, intellectual property and publication plans.

Output: a one-paragraph profile and a realistic availability window.

docs.title: 2. Build a shortlist · 3–5 months ahead
docs.text:
Choose approximately six to ten plausible routes, with several especially strong research matches. Include both centrally managed programs and direct laboratory postings when eligible. A route such as SULI may offer multiple hosts within one application; follow its current host-choice rules.

Record official URLs, job IDs, deadline timezones, reference deadlines and next actions in the tracker. Revisit the live posting before submitting. A program overview is not a live vacancy.

Output: a shortlist with eligibility confirmed or a clearly assigned question for the program office.

docs.title: 3. Map research fit · 2–4 months ahead
docs.text:
Find two or three groups per priority lab using official research pages and recent publications. For each group, write:

  • The research question you want to help investigate.
  • One recent project or paper, including a method or result you understand.
  • A skill you can contribute and a skill you want to learn.
  • A small, feasible summer-scale project direction or question.

Research fit is more useful than a famous laboratory name. Use the mentor outreach guide to decide whom to contact.

docs.title: 4. Request recommendations · ideally 4–6 weeks before due date
docs.text:
Ask people who have directly observed your work whether they can provide a strong, specific recommendation. Explain the program and deadline before entering their names into a portal. Give them an organized reference packet.

Request required transcripts early. Academic offices may take time to produce official copies. Check whether the portal accepts unofficial records.

docs.title: 5. Draft and tailor · 3–4 weeks before due date
docs.text:
Build a clear resume/CV and program-specific responses. Use this structure for your research story: problem → your action → evidence/result → next question → host fit. Follow the prompt, word limit and formatting exactly. Have a faculty mentor or writing-center reader check clarity and factual accuracy.

If you have no formal research, explain a concrete project, how you handled uncertainty, and what you learned. Do not invent expertise or results.

docs.title: 6. Submit and verify · aim for 2–3 days early
docs.text:
Check file readability, program/host names, job IDs, dates, enrollment details and recommendation status. Save submitted responses and confirmation. A saved draft is not a submitted application, and an invitation to a recommender is not a received letter.

Do not wait for a researcher’s reply to submit a complete application unless the program explicitly requires an established collaborator. SCGSR and faculty proposals require advance collaboration; SULI selection follows its own central process.

docs.title: 7. Interview and follow up
docs.text: Prepare a two-minute introduction, a five-minute project explanation and a few thoughtful questions about the work. Use the interview guide. Update your tracker after every contact, and respect the program’s published decision timeline.

docs.title: 8. Evaluate the written offer and prepare to arrive
docs.text: Confirm project scope, mentor, dates, funding, work location and onboarding conditions. Complete access and employment steps through official channels. Follow the arrival guide.

docs.text:
